choices: communicable disease
infectious disease
vector-borne transmission
contamination
questions.explanation: It spread from one person to another, which is what makes a disease communicable.
questions.question: Your patient has influenza and has been coughing in a small apartment where three family members also became sick this week. The illness passed from the patient to the family members in the home. What type of disease is this?

choices: communicable disease
bloodborne pathogens
airborne transmission
noncommunicable disease
questions.explanation: A communicable disease passes between people, so shared air, surfaces, and close contact in one wing can move it from resident to resident.
questions.question: A nursing home calls because six residents on one wing developed the same stomach virus over two days after sharing a dining room. The facility is asking how it moved between residents who never left the building. What kind of disease are they dealing with?

choices: communicable disease
exposure
indirect contact
infectious disease
questions.explanation: Chickenpox is communicable: it can be spread from one person to another, so every exposed classmate is at risk.
questions.question: Dispatch sends you to a school where a child with chickenpox has exposed an entire classroom. Your partner asks why the school nurse is sending exposure notices home to parents. What property of this illness makes the notices necessary?

choices: acute stress reaction
eustress
general adaptation syndrome
distress
questions.explanation: The stressor improved her performance instead of harming it, which is the definition of eustress.
questions.question: Before a difficult extrication, an EMT feels her heart rate climb and her focus sharpen. She performs better than usual and later says the pressure 'got her locked in.' What is this beneficial response to a stressor called?

choices: His stress response converted into burnout, a condition that develops over the course of a single shift
He was never having a stress response at all, and the second half of the shift is simply his normal personality
Arousal helps performance only up to a point; pushed past that point, the beneficial stress response tips over into distress
The first half of the shift was a delayed stress reaction, and it caught up with him all at once
questions.explanation: Nothing about the stressor changed except dose and duration: the same arousal that sharpened him early on kept climbing with no recovery, and past its useful peak it degrades performance instead of feeding it — that is the beneficial response (eustress) tipping into the harmful one (distress). Burnout is out: it builds over months to years of chronic stress, not one shift. A delayed stress reaction is a reaction that surfaces after a specific traumatic event, not a within-shift slide.
questions.question: An EMT starts a busy shift keyed up in a good way — alert, quick, and enjoying the pace. By hour ten, after back-to-back critical calls with no break, that same wired feeling has curdled: he is snapping at his partner, fumbling equipment he knows cold, and dreading the next tone. What best explains the change?

choices: Hypothalamus → pituitary gland → adrenal glands → cortisol
Hypothalamus → pituitary gland → adrenal glands → adrenaline
Hypothalamus → adrenal glands → pituitary gland → cortisol
Adrenal glands → pituitary gland → hypothalamus → cortisol
questions.explanation: The chain starts in the brain, so the hypothalamus fires first; it signals the pituitary, whose hormone (ACTH) travels in the blood to the adrenal glands, and the adrenal cortex answers with cortisol — the stress hormone this gland-to-gland chain exists to release. Adrenaline is the near miss: the adrenals do release it, but on a direct nerve signal, not as the end of the pituitary-driven hormone chain. The reversed and skipped-step chains break the one-signal-to-the-next order the stem describes.
questions.question: The surge that can sharpen a provider on a call runs on a hormone chain: the brain's alarm center starts it, one gland signals the next, and it ends at the adrenal glands, which release the body's main stress hormone into the blood. Which chain shows that pathway in the right order?

choices: immune
infection
contamination
exposure
questions.explanation: Her body can protect itself from acquiring measles again, which is exactly what being immune means.
questions.question: An EMT had measles as a child. She cares for a measles patient without becoming ill, because her body already knows how to fight that virus. What is her body's protective ability called?

choices: exposure
immune
infection
host
questions.explanation: Vaccination gave his body the ability to protect itself from acquiring hepatitis B, so he is immune to it.
questions.question: After completing his hepatitis B vaccine series and a titer showing antibodies, a paramedic is told his body can now defend itself against hepatitis B. What state has he achieved against that disease?

choices: pathogen
infectious disease
contamination
immune (immunity)
questions.explanation: The vaccine made his body able to protect itself from acquiring the disease, while his partner had no such protection.
questions.question: Two firefighters are exposed to the same patient with chickenpox. The one who had the varicella vaccine stays healthy; the one with no prior exposure or vaccine gets sick. What did the vaccine give the first firefighter?

choices: standard precautions
infection control
body substance isolation
personal protective equipment (PPE)
questions.explanation: Gloves, mask, and eye protection are equipment worn to block exposure to a pathogen, which is PPE.
questions.question: Before suctioning a patient who is coughing up blood, you put on gloves, a mask, and eye protection. What is the collective name for the gear you just put on?

choices: exposure control plan
personal protective equipment (PPE)
engineering controls
standard precautions
questions.explanation: Each item is protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or hazardous material, the definition of PPE.
questions.question: Your service issues gowns, gloves, and fit-tested respirators for calls involving a patient with suspected tuberculosis. What category of safety equipment do these items belong to?

choices: body substance isolation
personal protective equipment (PPE)
work practice controls
infection control
questions.explanation: The suit and gloves are protective equipment that blocks exposure to a hazardous material, which is PPE.
questions.question: At a scene with a spilled chemical, the hazmat officer stops you and says your turnout gear alone is not enough; you need the issued chemical suit and gloves before entry. What is he requiring you to wear?

choices: bloodborne pathogens
airborne pathogens
contamination
communicable disease
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus and HIV are pathogenic microorganisms present in human blood, which is the definition of bloodborne pathogens.
questions.question: While cleaning the ambulance, an EMT sticks her finger on a used IV needle left in the linen. The exposure concern is hepatitis B and HIV carried in the patient's blood. What group of microorganisms creates this risk?

choices: vector-borne transmission
bloodborne pathogens
infectious disease
standard precautions
questions.explanation: The plan targets disease-causing microorganisms present in human blood, namely bloodborne pathogens such as HBV and HIV.
questions.question: Your service's exposure control plan requires a hepatitis B vaccination offer and sharps containers in every unit because of microorganisms that live in human blood. What hazard is the plan built around?

choices: vector-borne pathogen
airborne pathogen
foodborne pathogen
bloodborne pathogen
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C is a pathogenic microorganism present in human blood that can cause disease in humans, a bloodborne pathogen.
questions.question: A patient with hepatitis C is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. Your partner reminds you to glove up and watch for splashes because the virus travels in blood. What is hepatitis C classified as?

choices: vector
host
pathogen
carrier
questions.explanation: The mouse is the organism the infecting agent lives in and attacks, which makes it the host.
questions.question: A tick picks up the Lyme disease bacterium while feeding on an infected white-footed mouse, then later bites a hiker. In the first part of that chain, what role does the mouse play for the bacterium?

choices: vector
contamination
host
pathogen
questions.explanation: The patient is the individual attacked by the infecting agent, which is the definition of a host.
questions.question: Your patient is a teenager whose body the influenza virus has invaded and is now producing fever and aches. In infection terms, what is the patient in relation to the virus?

choices: pathogen
reservoir
host
vector
questions.explanation: She is the organism the infecting agent lives in, a host, even though she has no symptoms.
questions.question: A cook carries typhoid bacteria in her gallbladder for years without ever feeling sick, while the bacteria live off her body. What is she, biologically, to those bacteria?

choices: Documenting the possible exposure in the run report after the call is over
Hand hygiene and disinfecting the stretcher and equipment between patients
Asking the patient to hold his breath while you load him into the ambulance
Putting on a mask only after the patient has already coughed in the unit
questions.explanation: The travel link is the organism's ride from one host to the next — on hands, gloves, a stretcher rail, a blood pressure cuff. Washing hands and disinfecting equipment between patients cuts that ride, which is why it stops spread even though the organism and the carrier are unchanged. Documentation happens after the trip is over and breaks nothing; a mask put on after the cough is protection that starts after the travel already happened; and a patient cannot hold his breath through a call.
questions.question: A communicable disease travels along a chain: the organism leaves the person or place it lives in, moves by some route, and enters a new host. Your crew cannot change the organism, and you cannot change the patient who is carrying it. Which crew action breaks the chain at the travel link?

choices: Both illnesses are communicable because both involve microorganisms
The wound infection is infectious but not communicable; measles is both
Neither illness is infectious, because one needs a cut and the other needs a cough
Measles is infectious but not communicable, because it spreads through the air
questions.explanation: Infectious means organisms have invaded the body. Communicable adds that the disease can spread from one person or species to another: the wound infection stays with its host, while measles passes between people, including through the air.
questions.question: Two patients are discussed at a training night. The first has a bacterial wound infection that began when organisms entered a cut; it cannot pass to anyone else. The second has measles, which spreads readily from person to person. Which statement is correct?

choices: Skip respiratory precautions for patients with no fever, because a person without symptoms cannot spread disease.
Treat every patient as potentially infectious, because a carrier of a communicable disease may have no symptoms at all.
Rely on dispatch screening to flag infectious patients before arrival, since carriers are identified in advance.
Take full precautions only with patients who look or feel sick, since carriers usually show some symptoms.
questions.explanation: A carrier of a communicable disease may have no symptoms, so every patient is treated as potentially infectious.
questions.question: In 1907, New York cook Mary Mallon was identified as the first known healthy carrier of typhoid fever in the United States. Investigators linked her cooking to about 57 typhoid infections and 3 deaths, yet she never felt sick herself. What should an EMT take from this case when deciding on precautions?

choices: Assume any contact with the infected patient's body fluids during care is an exposure until proven otherwise.
Body fluids only become infectious after the patient's symptoms have peaked, so early care is low risk.
Routine gloves alone eliminate the risk, because hospital transmission of fluid-borne disease is not possible.
Exposure only counts if a sharps injury occurred, since intact skin contact with fluids is harmless.
questions.explanation: For a communicable disease carried in body fluids, any fluid contact during care is an exposure until proven otherwise.
questions.question: In fall 2014, Thomas Eric Duncan, who had traveled from Liberia, was treated for Ebola at a Dallas hospital. Two nurses who cared for him, Nina Pham and Amber Vinson, became infected, the first Ebola transmissions on US soil. What does this case teach about caring for a patient with a disease carried in body fluids?

choices: The first EMT's alarm system never actually fired, which is why she stayed calm and effective
Only the second EMT released stress hormones; the first one's body skipped the stress response entirely
The difference is physical fitness, because the stress response is purely physical and thinking plays no part in it
The appraisal step — how the thinking brain reads the alarm — decides whether arousal becomes a helpful challenge response or a harmful threat response
questions.explanation: Both bodies fired the same alarm — both felt the surge — so the difference cannot be whether stress hormones were released; it has to be what happened next. The brain's appraisal of the alarm is the fork in the road: read as a challenge the arousal can handle, it becomes the beneficial response; read as a threat, it becomes the harmful one. That is why the same call can leave one provider sharper and the other rattled, and why appraisal — not fitness or a missing alarm — is the mechanism.
questions.question: Two EMTs draw the same tough assignment. The first feels the surge, sizes the job up as a challenge she can handle, and settles into sharp, focused work. The second reads the same surge as a threat, fixates on everything that could go wrong, and tightens up until his performance suffers. What best explains why the same body alarm produced two different outcomes?

choices: Arousal read as readiness feeds the beneficial stress response; fighting to force calm works against the same chemistry instead of using it
High arousal always improves performance, so the officer should add even more pressure to the drill
The buzz means the rookie is having an acute stress reaction and should be pulled from the drill
Calming down is impossible for a new provider, so officers should never address a rookie's nerves at all
questions.explanation: The rookie's arousal is not the problem — arousal is the raw fuel of the beneficial stress response, and reading it as readiness ('this is my body getting ready') points it toward performance, while struggling to suppress it adds a second fight on top of the first. The buzz alone is not an acute stress reaction, which is a response to a traumatic event, not pre-drill nerves. And arousal does not help without limit — past its peak it tips into distress — so piling on more pressure would be the wrong move.
questions.question: A training officer watches a rookie get wired before a full-scale drill — hands buzzing, talking fast, clearly amped up. Instead of telling her to calm down, the officer says, 'Good — that buzz is your body getting ready. Use it.' Why is that coaching sound?

choices: Postpone the test until he feels fully calm, since a calm state is required for good performance.
Reframe the racing heart as fuel for performance, because viewing arousal as useful turns it toward eustress.
Suppress the arousal completely before starting, because any arousal during testing lowers scores.
Ignore the sensation and hope it passes, because mindset about arousal has no measurable effect.
questions.explanation: Telling yourself the racing heart is fuel measurably improves performance; the reframe produces eustress.
questions.question: In a 2010 experiment, students preparing for the GRE were told that bodily arousal during testing actually improves performance. That group scored higher on the lab GRE math section and, months later, on their real GRE. An EMT feels his heart racing before a skills test. What does this research support doing?

choices: Fight to calm down first, because lowering arousal is the only proven way to perform well under pressure.
Avoid the high-pressure assignment until the anxiety fades on its own over time.
Relabel the anxiety as excitement, since both are high-arousal states and the relabel converts stress into a beneficial response.
Treat the anxiety as a warning sign of an acute stress reaction that requires removal from the call.
questions.explanation: Saying 'I am excited' instead of fighting to calm down is an evidence-based way to make stress work for you.
questions.question: Harvard researcher Alison Wood Brooks studied karaoke singing, public speaking, and math performance in 2014. Participants who said 'I am excited' before performing did better than those who tried to calm down. What technique does this case illustrate for an EMT facing a high-pressure call?

choices: Memory cells that recognize the virus and launch a rapid, stronger antibody response
A small amount of live virus stored in her blood, keeping her mildly infected ever since
Antibodies that stay at full strength in her blood for life without ever fading
A thicker skin barrier that keeps the virus from entering her body in the first place
questions.explanation: Speed is the clue in the stem: a first encounter is slow because the immune system has to learn the virus from scratch. The vaccine ran that lesson in advance and left memory cells behind; on the real exposure they recognize the virus and produce antibodies fast and in force, ending the infection before symptoms start. Antibodies themselves fade over time — it is the memory cells, not a lifetime stockpile of antibody, that persist — and no live virus sits stored in her blood.
questions.question: Years after her chickenpox vaccination, an EMT is exposed to the virus on a call. Her body shuts the virus down before she ever feels sick — and handles it noticeably faster than it could have the very first time it met that virus. What did the vaccine leave behind that makes the second response faster?

choices: She is now a carrier and should be kept off patient care
The vaccine gave her the disease in a mild form
She is protected anyway, because receiving the shots is what matters
She cannot count on being protected from the disease and needs follow-up, which may include another vaccine series
questions.explanation: Being protected means the body can keep itself from acquiring the disease. Without antibodies she has not developed that protection, so occupational health follows up instead of assuming she is covered.
questions.question: A medic completes the hepatitis B vaccine series, but her follow-up blood test shows no protective antibodies. What does this mean for her status?

choices: Immunity only develops after a person survives the actual disease, never from a milder related infection.
Vaccination works by treating an active infection after symptoms have already appeared.
Immunity can be built before exposure, which is the entire basis of the vaccines EMTs are required to keep current.
Prior exposure offers no real protection, so the boy's recovery was simply a matter of chance.
questions.explanation: Immunity can be built before exposure; that is the basis of vaccination.
questions.question: On May 14, 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox material from a dairymaid. When Jenner deliberately exposed the boy to smallpox weeks later, Phipps did not develop the disease. What principle did this first vaccination demonstrate?

choices: Standard precautions can be relaxed, because a patient kept in isolation is already protected from germs.
Providers need no protective equipment, since the patient's condition is genetic rather than contagious to the crew.
Strict infection control around an immunocompromised patient is not optional, because the patient has no immune safety net.
The patient's own antibodies will handle minor exposures, so brief lapses in technique carry little risk.
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised patients have no safety net; strict infection control around them is not optional.
questions.question: David Vetter, born in 1971 with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), lived in a sterile isolator at Texas Children's Hospital because his immune system could not fight infection; germ-free isolation was the only protection available to him. What does his case mean for EMTs caring for an immunocompromised patient?

choices: engineering controls
standard precautions
infection control procedures
personal protective equipment
questions.explanation: The gloves, mask, and eye protection are physical barriers worn to block exposure to a pathogen, which is personal protective equipment. Standard precautions are the rules that tell you when to wear them, not the gear itself.
questions.question: Before suctioning a patient with a bleeding mouth injury, you put on gloves, a mask, and eye protection. These items are all examples of:

choices: The self-sheathing needle in the sharps kit
The standing rule that every patient's blood is treated as infectious
The ambulance's ventilation system
The gloves and goggles you are wearing
questions.explanation: Personal protective equipment is the gear worn to block exposure, here the gloves and goggles. The treat-all-blood rule is standard precautions, and the self-sheathing needle is an engineering control built into the equipment.
questions.question: On one call, three different protections are in play: the gloves and goggles you are wearing, the standing rule that every patient's blood is treated as infectious, and the self-sheathing needle in the sharps kit. Which of these is the equipment worn to block exposure?

choices: PPE is only as good as its weakest gap, and removal is the most dangerous step, so use a buddy check when doffing.
A small area of exposed skin is acceptable as long as the respirator and gloves fit correctly.
Doffing quickly is safest, because speed reduces the time spent near contaminated equipment.
Once the patient is stabilized, PPE gaps no longer matter because the exposure window has passed.
questions.explanation: One exposed gap defeats the whole barrier; removal is the most dangerous step and needs a buddy check.
questions.question: During the 2014 Dallas Ebola response, the PPE worn by nurses caring for patient Thomas Eric Duncan left areas of the neck exposed, and two nurses became infected. The CDC then revised its guidance to require full coverage with no skin showing and a trained observer for doffing. What is the lesson for an EMT donning PPE?

choices: Touching the face during removal is low risk, since the outside of the gloves stays clean during care.
Treat used PPE as contaminated waste and doff slowly and deliberately, with hand hygiene as part of the protection.
Remove PPE as fast as possible once care ends, because the danger ends when the suit comes off.
Skip hand hygiene after doffing if the gloves show no visible tears or contamination.
questions.explanation: The failure came at removal; used PPE is contaminated waste, and slow, deliberate doffing with hand hygiene is part of the protection.
questions.question: Spanish nursing assistant Teresa Romero cared for a missionary who died of Ebola in September 2014. She became the first person known to contract Ebola outside West Africa; investigators believed she touched her face with a contaminated glove while removing her protective suit. What practice does her case demand?

choices: Hepatitis C has a vaccine but hepatitis B does not, which is why OSHA requires employers to offer the hepatitis C vaccine free
All three viruses attack the liver, and all three can be prevented with vaccines
HIV attacks the liver the way the hepatitis viruses do, while hepatitis B attacks the immune system
Hepatitis B and hepatitis C attack the liver and travel in blood; HIV attacks the immune system's CD4 cells and also travels in blood — and of the three, only hepatitis B has a vaccine
questions.explanation: The three share a route — blood — but not a target. The hepatitis viruses live in the liver; HIV lives in the immune system itself, destroying the CD4 helper cells that coordinate the body's defenses. The vaccine fact follows the same split: a hepatitis B vaccine exists (it is the one OSHA requires employers to offer free), while there is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV — hepatitis C's protection is avoidance, and its treatment is a cure, not a vaccine. Swapping the targets or the vaccine between them is exactly the error the plan exists to prevent.
questions.question: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires every employer to keep a written Exposure Control Plan for the hazards that ride in human blood. Three of those hazards sit side by side in the plan. Which statement about them is correct?

choices: He is right; only hepatitis B requires gloves
Hepatitis C travels in blood, so it belongs to the group of bloodborne hazards, and gloves are required for any blood contact
Gloves matter for hepatitis A, not hepatitis C
Gloves are needed only if the EMT has an open cut
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C is carried in blood, which puts it among the bloodborne pathogens the precautions are built for. The organ the virus damages does not change how it can reach you.
questions.question: Your partner says, 'This patient's hepatitis C is a liver disease, so gloves are probably overkill for a nosebleed.' What is the best correction?

choices: Blood products carried risk only for hemophilia patients, not for anyone receiving a transfusion.
Hemophilia itself causes HIV infection, independent of any blood product the patient receives.
HIV spreads mainly through casual contact, which is why White's school barred him from attending.
A bloodborne pathogen can ride a blood product or any blood exposure, so no blood exposure should ever be treated as trivial.
questions.explanation: Blood is a vehicle for bloodborne pathogens; White's infection came entirely through a blood product.
questions.question: Teenager Ryan White was diagnosed with HIV in 1984 at age 13 after being infected through contaminated factor VIII blood product used to treat his hemophilia; he had no other risk factor. What does his case illustrate about bloodborne pathogens?

choices: Recap used needles before disposal to conserve space in the sharps container.
Fill sharps containers above the line during busy shifts and empty them at the end of the week.
Carry a used needle to the container by hand if the container is more than a few steps away.
Never overfill a sharps container and never carry a used needle loose; dispose of sharps properly every time.
questions.explanation: One used needle carried two bloodborne pathogens; never overfill a sharps container or carry a used needle loose.
questions.question: In July 1998, nurse Karen Daley was stuck by a needle protruding from an overfilled sharps container at Brigham and Women's Hospital. That single needlestick infected her with both HIV and hepatitis C, and her advocacy led to the federal Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act. What sharps practice does her case demand of EMTs?

choices: The mice and the hikers are hosts; the ticks are vectors
The ticks are hosts; the mice are vectors
The bacteria are the vector; the ticks are the pathogen
The hikers are the reservoir; the bacteria are the host
questions.explanation: Hosts are the organisms the agent lives in or attacks: the mice the bacteria live in, and the hikers they ultimately infect. The ticks only transport the bacteria, which makes them vectors, and the bacteria are the pathogen.
questions.question: Health officials map a Lyme disease chain in a county park: the bacteria live in white-footed mice, ticks carry the bacteria between animals, and hikers end up sick. Which pairing is correct?

choices: The outbreak spread only from person to person, so animal hosts played no real role in transmission.
Ask about animal exposures during assessment, because the host chain behind a patient's illness often runs through animals first.
Animal contact is irrelevant to a human infection history once the patient shows symptoms.
The pigs were the original natural reservoir, so only pig exposure needs to be asked about.
questions.explanation: Nipah reached humans through two kinds of host, so animal exposure history matters on assessment.
questions.question: In the 1998-99 Nipah outbreak in Malaysia, Pteropus fruit bats were the natural reservoir hosts of the virus, and domestic pigs became amplifying hosts that caught it from bats and passed it to farm workers, causing 265 human cases. What does this host chain mean for patient assessment?

choices: Only adult tick bites, because larval ticks cannot carry the bacterium from the mouse host.
Time spent in open water and at beaches, since Lyme risk is highest in aquatic environments.
Whether a mouse bit him directly, since mice pass Lyme disease to people themselves.
Time spent clearing brush and leaf litter at the wooded edge of his own yard, where the host mice nest and the ticks that fed on them wait.
questions.explanation: The chain runs mouse to tick to person, and the stem places the mice in leaf litter and brush at the woods' edge — so exposure can happen during yard work there, no hiking required. Mice do not pass Lyme disease to people directly; the tick does.
questions.question: The white-footed mouse is the principal reservoir host of Borrelia burgdorferi, the Lyme disease bacterium, in the northeastern United States. These mice nest in leaf litter and brush along the edges of woods. Larval blacklegged ticks feed on the mice, pick up the bacterium, and later feed on people. A man with suspected Lyme disease says he never hikes and has not been in deep woods. Following the chain in this case, which part of his history should you ask more about?
